summary.text: A 47-year-old man with no systemic comorbidities had been diagnosed with juvenile open-angle glaucoma in both eyes at age 22. At presentation his visual acuity was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/12 in the left, with IOP of 38 and 40 mmHg, a cup-disc ratio of 0.7 and bayonetting. He started triple topical therapy, declined filtering surgery and defaulted on follow-up for three years.

On re-presentation he reported progressive visual deterioration, with VA of 6/48 OD and 6/60 OS and IOP of 36 and 43 mmHg. Four topical agents were recommended and he later had trabeculectomy in both eyes. The left eye developed panophthalmitis with no light perception and was eviscerated. The right eye had bleb failure and a Baerveldt device, then a second device after IOP rose.

Six years after the second device, the superonasal tube became exposed (3.8 mm), with visual acuity of counting fingers at 3 feet, IOP 11 mmHg and no leakage or intraocular infection. An initial amniotic membrane transplant failed, leaving 3.2 mm of exposure. Conservative management included serum drops, topical antibiotics, oral doxycycline and a bandage contact lens; a scleral lens then reduced exposure to 1.0 mm over six months, but it rose to 2.0 mm by eight months.

Surgical repair used a 3 × 3 mm corneal patch graft secured with 9-0 nylon sutures and a double-layer amniotic membrane anchored with 10-0 nylon. The tube was fully covered on day 1, re-epithelialisation was complete by eight weeks and the tube remained covered at six months. At 12 months there was no recurrence of tube exposure or conjunctival erosion and IOP was stable, and he remains under follow-up.
